metadata.description: Medical knowledge base for MedGuard RAG Agent — patient vitals evaluation and emergency first aid

heart_rate.notes: Resting HR. Athletes may have lower baseline (40-60 bpm) without pathology.

spo2.notes: SpO2 has no high-end concern. Values below 90% require immediate intervention.

condition_patterns.name: Hypoxia / Respiratory Distress
condition_patterns.description: Low blood oxygen combined with fast breathing suggests the body is struggling to oxygenate. May indicate respiratory distress, asthma attack, pneumonia, or early heart failure.

condition_patterns.name: Circulatory Shock
condition_patterns.description: Rapid heart rate with dangerously low blood pressure. Organs are not receiving adequate blood flow. Life-threatening — requires immediate emergency response.

condition_patterns.name: Suspected Cardiac Event (Heart Attack)
condition_patterns.description: Combination of abnormal HR, BP, and low SpO2 may indicate myocardial infarction (heart attack). Time-critical — every minute counts.

condition_patterns.name: Cardiac Arrest
condition_patterns.description: Near-absent vitals suggest cardiac arrest. Patient is likely unconscious and not breathing. CPR must begin immediately.

condition_patterns.name: Hypoglycemia (Low Blood Sugar)
condition_patterns.description: Low blood glucose with elevated HR. Patient may feel confused, shaky, or faint. Below 50 mg/dL is an emergency — brain function is at risk.

condition_patterns.name: Hyperglycemia / Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
condition_patterns.description: Very high glucose with fast breathing (Kussmaul breathing) may indicate DKA in diabetic patients. Requires urgent medical attention.

condition_patterns.name: Hypertensive Crisis
condition_patterns.description: Extremely high blood pressure can cause stroke, heart attack, or organ damage. Patient must rest and be seen by a doctor immediately.

condition_patterns.name: Suspected Sepsis
condition_patterns.description: High/low temperature combined with fast HR and breathing is a classic sepsis triad. Sepsis is life-threatening and requires immediate hospitalization.

condition_patterns.name: Hypothermia
condition_patterns.description: Body temperature is dangerously low. Core body functions begin to slow down. Critical below 32°C.

actions: Open windows or doors to improve ventilation and fresh air flow
Have the patient sit upright or lean slightly forward — do not lay flat
Remove any tight clothing around chest or neck
Avoid any physical exertion
If patient has a prescribed inhaler, assist them in using it
Monitor SpO2 closely every 2-3 minutes
If SpO2 drops below 90% or patient feels worse — call emergency services immediately
Move patient to a warm indoor environment
Apply warm blankets, focus on covering the torso and neck
If conscious and able to swallow: offer warm (not hot) drinks
Avoid direct heat sources like electric heaters directly on skin
Monitor temperature every 10 minutes
Remove excess clothing and heavy blankets
Apply cool (not cold) damp cloth to forehead, neck, and wrists
Encourage fluid intake — water or oral rehydration solution
Ensure the room is well-ventilated
Paracetamol (acetaminophen) can help reduce fever if not contraindicated
Seek medical advice if fever persists more than 48 hours or exceeds 39.5°C
Have the patient rest in a quiet, calm environment
Encourage slow, deep breathing (4 seconds in, 4 seconds out)
Avoid caffeine, stimulants, and physical activity
Do NOT give extra blood pressure medication without medical instruction
Recheck BP in 15-20 minutes
If BP exceeds 180 mmHg — call emergency services
Give 15g of fast-acting carbohydrates immediately: fruit juice (150ml), glucose tablets, or 3-4 teaspoons of sugar dissolved in water
Have patient sit or lie down
Recheck blood glucose after 15 minutes
If glucose remains low: repeat carbohydrate intake
Once glucose normalizes: give a small snack (crackers, bread) to maintain levels
If patient becomes confused or loses consciousness — call emergency services immediately and do NOT give anything orally
Ask patient to consciously slow their breathing
Guide them through diaphragmatic breathing: breathe in slowly for 4 seconds, hold 2 seconds, out for 6 seconds
Have patient sit upright
Reduce anxiety and stress in the environment — stay calm, speak reassuringly
Ensure the room has good ventilation
Monitor for worsening — if rate exceeds 28 or patient struggles to breathe, call emergency services

heart_attack.triggers: Abnormal HR + elevated or low BP + low SpO2 + possible chest pain
steps: Call emergency services (112 or your local emergency number) IMMEDIATELY — do not wait
Have the patient stop all activity and sit or lie in a semi-reclined position (not flat)
Loosen any tight clothing: collar, tie, belt
If the patient is conscious, not allergic to aspirin, and can swallow: give 300mg Aspirin — have them chew it, not swallow whole
Stay with the patient, speak calmly, and reassure them — stress makes the heart work harder
Do not give food or water
If the patient loses consciousness and stops breathing — begin CPR immediately (see cardiac_arrest protocol)

cardiac_arrest.triggers: Very low HR (<30 bpm), very low BP, very low SpO2, patient unconscious and not breathing
steps: Call emergency services IMMEDIATELY — put the phone on speaker so you can follow instructions
Check if the patient is conscious: tap shoulders and shout 'Are you okay?'
Check for breathing: look for chest movement for no more than 10 seconds
If not breathing normally — begin CPR immediately:
- Place heel of hand on center of chest (lower half of breastbone)
- Place other hand on top, interlace fingers
- Push down HARD and FAST — at least 5cm depth, 100-120 times per minute
- After 30 compressions: give 2 rescue breaths (tilt head back, pinch nose, seal mouth, breathe in for 1 second)
- Repeat 30:2 cycle continuously until help arrives
If an AED (defibrillator) is nearby: send someone to get it — turn it on and follow the audio instructions
Do not stop CPR until paramedics arrive and take over
Call emergency services immediately
Sit the patient upright — leaning slightly forward ('tripod position') helps open the airways
Open all windows and doors to maximize fresh air in the room
Loosen any tight clothing around chest, neck, or abdomen
If the patient has a prescribed inhaler (e.g. for asthma) — help them use it now
Do NOT give food or water
Do NOT leave the patient alone
If patient loses consciousness — place in recovery position (on their side) and monitor breathing

severe_hypoglycemia.triggers: Blood glucose < 50 mg/dL, possible confusion or loss of consciousness
steps: Call emergency services if patient is confused, cannot swallow safely, or unconscious
If patient is conscious and can swallow: give glucose gel, fruit juice (150ml), or sugary drink immediately
Do NOT give anything orally if patient is unconscious or cannot swallow — choking risk
If a glucagon emergency kit is available and you are trained to use it — administer it now
Place unconscious patient in recovery position (on their side) to protect airway
Stay with patient and monitor breathing and consciousness
Recheck glucose every 5 minutes if meter is available

hypertensive_crisis.triggers: Systolic BP >= 180 mmHg or diastolic BP >= 120 mmHg
steps: Call emergency services
Have the patient stop all activity immediately and sit or lie down in a quiet room
Loosen tight clothing
Keep the environment calm — reduce noise, light, and stress
Do NOT give extra blood pressure medications without direct medical instruction
Watch for stroke symptoms: facial drooping, arm weakness, slurred speech — if present, tell emergency services immediately
Do not give food, water, or stimulants (coffee, cigarettes)

sepsis.triggers: High/low temperature + heart rate > 120 + respiratory rate > 25
steps: Call emergency services immediately — sepsis can become fatal within hours
Note the time symptoms started — this is critical information for doctors
Keep patient warm and as comfortable as possible
Do not give food or water
Monitor breathing and consciousness continuously
If patient has prescribed antibiotics and doctor has authorized early self-administration — follow those instructions
